subject: Inglês
title: Morphology: Word formation
aliases: Conversion and zero derivation in English
Word families and parts of speech

scope.covers: Processos de formação de palavras em inglês: base, raiz e afixos; prefixação e sufixação; derivação e flexão; mudança de classe e conversão; composição; clipping, blending, acrônimos e iniciais; retroformação; alterações ortográficas frequentes e pistas de classe gramatical no contexto.

theoryTitle: Como as palavras inglesas são formadas

chapters.title: 1. Base, afixos e derivação
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

Em questões de inglês, muitas vezes o candidato conhece a palavra-base, mas precisa reconhecer uma forma relacionada que completa a frase. Saber que *care* é substantivo ou verbo ajuda a compreender *careful*, *careless* e *carefully*. A morfologia estuda as partes das palavras e os processos que criam formas lexicais.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Base**: forma à qual se acrescenta um elemento, como *kind* em *unkindness*.
> - **Raiz**: núcleo lexical que carrega o significado central.
> - **Afixo**: elemento preso a uma base; pode ser prefixo ou sufixo.
> - **Prefixo**: afixo colocado antes da base.
> - **Sufixo**: afixo colocado depois da base.
> - **Derivação**: criação de uma palavra relacionada, muitas vezes com mudança de sentido ou classe.

### Prefixos: antes da base

Prefixos normalmente alteram o sentido sem mudar a classe gramatical: *happy* (adjetivo) → *unhappy* (adjetivo); *agree* (verbo) → *disagree* (verbo). Alguns sentidos recorrentes são negação ou oposição (*un-* em *unfair*, *dis-* em *dislike*), repetição (*re-* em *rewrite*), anterioridade (*pre-* em *prewar*) e excesso (*over-* em *overcook*). O sentido depende da palavra: *in-* aparece com variantes como *im-* em *impossible* e *il-* em *illegal*. Não se deve concluir que toda palavra iniciada por essas letras contém o mesmo prefixo: *uncle*, por exemplo, não é formado por *un-* + *cle*.

### Sufixos: depois da base

Sufixos são especialmente úteis para identificar a classe provável da palavra. *Employ* → *employer* (substantivo, pessoa); *develop* → *development* (substantivo); *create* → *creative* (adjetivo); *quick* → *quickly* (advérbio); *modern* → *modernize* (verbo). A relação não é uma fórmula sem exceções: a palavra precisa caber no sentido e na gramática da frase.

| Sufixo | Classe frequentemente formada | Exemplo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-er*, *-ment*, *-ness* | substantivo | *teach → teacher; improve → improvement; kind → kindness* |
| *-ful*, *-less*, *-able* | adjetivo | *care → careful/careless; read → readable* |
| *-ly* | advérbio | *slow → slowly* |
| *-ize*, *-ify*, *-en* | verbo | *modern → modernize; simple → simplify; wide → widen* |

### Derivação e flexão não são a mesma coisa

Derivação cria um item lexical relacionado e pode mudar a classe: *happy* (adjetivo) → *happiness* (substantivo). Flexão adapta uma palavra às exigências gramaticais sem criar, em geral, uma nova entrada lexical: *work* → *works* (terceira pessoa), *worked* (passado), *working* (forma em *-ing*); *book* → *books* (plural). Em *workers*, por exemplo, *-er* deriva *worker* (“trabalhador”) de *work*, enquanto *-s* marca o plural: há derivação e depois flexão.

### Grafia ao acrescentar sufixos

Há ajustes ortográficos comuns. Em muitos casos, o *y* final precedido de consoante passa a *i*: *happy → happiness*, *beauty → beautiful*. O *e* final pode cair diante de certos sufixos: *create → creation*, *use → useful*. Às vezes a consoante final dobra, como em *begin → beginner*. Essas tendências não substituem a consulta ao vocabulário: *enjoy → enjoyable* mantém o *y*, pois antes dele há vogal.

### Como cai na prova

- A posição do afixo ajuda: prefixo antes, sufixo depois.
- Um sufixo pode indicar a classe que falta: após *very*, espera-se normalmente adjetivo ou advérbio; após artigo, é comum um substantivo.
- Verifique se a questão pede significado ou classe: *un-* muda o sentido; *-ness* transforma *kind* em substantivo.
- Não confunda plural ou tempo verbal com derivação: *cats* e *walked* são formas flexionadas.

chapters.title: 2. Composição e mudança de classe
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

Nem toda palavra complexa contém um prefixo ou sufixo. Em *toothbrush*, duas bases se combinam; em *to email*, um substantivo passa a ser usado como verbo sem afixo visível. Reconhecer esses padrões evita classificar toda palavra longa como derivada por afixação.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Composição (compounding)**: combinação de duas ou mais bases para formar uma unidade lexical.
> - **Composto**: palavra ou expressão lexical resultante da composição.
> - **Conversão**: uso de uma forma em outra classe sem afixo manifesto; também chamada derivação zero.
> - **Classe gramatical**: categoria como substantivo, verbo, adjetivo ou advérbio.

### Composição: duas bases, uma unidade

Exemplos claros são *tooth + brush → toothbrush*, *rain + coat → raincoat*, *black + board → blackboard* e *home + work → homework*. A combinação pode ser escrita junta, separada (*ice cream*) ou com hífen (*well-known*). A grafia, por si só, não determina se os elementos formam um composto: observe a unidade de sentido e confirme em dicionário quando houver dúvida.

Compostos aparecem em diferentes classes: substantivos (*bus stop*, *washing machine*), adjetivos (*snow-white*, *user-friendly*) e verbos (*babysit*, *stir-fry*). Em compostos nominais do tipo substantivo + substantivo, o elemento final costuma indicar a categoria principal: *toothbrush* é um tipo de *brush*, e *raincoat* é um tipo de *coat*. O primeiro elemento restringe ou especifica o segundo.

A tonicidade também pode ajudar, mas não é uma regra infalível. Em muitos compostos nominais, a primeira parte recebe mais destaque: *BLACKbird* (a espécie de pássaro) pode contrastar com *black BIRD* (qualquer pássaro preto). A pronúncia e o contexto resolvem casos em que a grafia é igual.

### Conversão: a forma muda de função

Na conversão, uma forma passa a desempenhar outra classe sem mudança visível: *email* é substantivo em *I sent an email* e verbo em *Email me the file*; *water* é substantivo em *some water* e verbo em *water the plants*; *clean* pode ser adjetivo em *a clean room* e verbo em *clean the room*. A função sintática e as palavras vizinhas revelam o uso. Isso não significa que toda palavra tenha todas as classes possíveis: é o uso convencional e o contexto que importam.

### Como distinguir processos

| Exemplo | Processo | Evidência |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *unfair* | prefixação | *un-* antes da base *fair* |
| *kindness* | sufixação derivacional | *-ness* depois de *kind*; adjetivo vira substantivo |
| *toothbrush* | composição | *tooth* e *brush* se combinam |
| *to bottle* | conversão | *bottle* passa de substantivo a verbo sem afixo |
| *books* | flexão | *-s* marca plural, sem criar lexema novo |

### Como cai na prova

- Se duas bases permanecem reconhecíveis, considere composição.
- Se a mesma forma aparece como substantivo e verbo sem mudança gráfica, investigue conversão.
- A classe deve ser inferida pelo contexto: em *They water the garden*, *water* é verbo porque recebe objeto e expressa ação.
- Não use apenas hífen ou espaço para decidir: compostos podem ter grafias diferentes.

chapters.title: 3. Redução, mistura, siglas e retroformação
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

O vocabulário também cresce por encurtamento ou fusão de formas. *Advertisement* pode ser reduzido a *ad*; *brunch* combina partes de *breakfast* e *lunch*. Em prova, o desafio é identificar de onde veio a forma e distinguir processos que parecem semelhantes.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Clipping (redução)**: encurtamento de uma palavra, sem combinação necessária com outra.
> - **Blending (cruzamento vocabular)**: fusão de segmentos de duas palavras, com sobreposição ou perda de partes.
> - **Acronym (acrônimo)**: forma criada com letras iniciais e pronunciada como palavra.
> - **Initialism (sigla por soletração)**: sequência de iniciais pronunciadas letra por letra.
> - **Back-formation (retroformação)**: criação de uma palavra mais curta pela remoção de uma parte interpretada como afixo.

### Clipping: uma palavra encurtada

*Laboratory → lab*, *advertisement → ad*, *examination → exam* e *telephone → phone* são reduções. A forma curta mantém o núcleo do significado e costuma ser mais informal ou conveniente. A redução não exige duas bases: por isso *lab* não é blending. Há reduções no começo (*phone*), no fim (*exam*) ou com outras alterações de forma.

### Blending: partes fundidas

*Breakfast + lunch → brunch* conserva segmentos de ambas as bases; *smoke + fog → smog* também. *Motel* combina *motor* e *hotel*. A pista decisiva é a fusão parcial, em vez da preservação integral das duas palavras como num composto comum.

### Acronyms e initialisms

*NATO* é normalmente pronunciado como uma palavra e, por isso, é acrônimo. *BBC* é pronunciado letra por letra e é initialism. A forma gráfica em maiúsculas não basta para decidir: considere a pronúncia. Algumas formas podem virar palavras comuns e perder maiúsculas no uso, como *laser*.

### Back-formation: remoção que cria uma base

Em *editor → edit*, retirou-se a terminação que parecia um sufixo para formar um verbo. *Donation → donate* e *babysitter → babysit* são outros exemplos frequentemente analisados como retroformação. A direção é importante: na retroformação, a forma percebida como mais simples é criada a partir da mais longa; não se trata apenas de acrescentar um sufixo, como em *teach → teacher*.

### Como cai na prova

- Uma só palavra encurtada: clipping (*exam*).
- Segmentos de duas palavras unidos: blending (*brunch*).
- Iniciais pronunciadas como palavra ou letra a letra: acronym ou initialism.
- Forma curta criada pela remoção de um elemento interpretado como sufixo: back-formation (*edit* de *editor*).
- Composição preserva bases inteiras com mais frequência; blending funde apenas partes.

chapters.title: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

Exercícios de *word formation* frequentemente apresentam uma palavra-base entre parênteses e uma lacuna: *Her answer was ___ (LOGIC).* É preciso formar *logical*, mas também verificar se a lacuna exige adjetivo. A terminação sozinha não resolve a questão: sentido, classe e grafia precisam funcionar juntos.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Word family**: conjunto de palavras relacionadas a uma base, como *decide, decision, decisive, decisively*.
> - **Part of speech**: classe gramatical exigida pelo papel da palavra na frase.
> - **Collocation**: combinação convencional de palavras, como *make a decision*.
> - **Stress**: destaque de uma sílaba na pronúncia.

### Método em quatro verificações

1. Leia a frase inteira para identificar a ideia: positiva, negativa, pessoa, ação ou qualidade.
2. Observe a posição da lacuna e determine a classe: depois de *a/an/the* pode vir substantivo; antes de substantivo pode vir adjetivo; depois de verbo, pode ser advérbio ou complemento.
3. Escolha um processo ou afixo que produza a classe e o sentido necessários: *care → careful* para qualidade, *carefully* para modo, *carelessness* para substantivo negativo.
4. Confira a grafia e a combinação usual. *Success* dá *successful* e *successfully*, mas *succeed* é o verbo; *economic* e *economical* são adjetivos com sentidos distintos.

### A classe depende da frase

Compare *a daily newspaper* (adjetivo: diário) e *I read the newspaper daily* (advérbio: todos os dias). Em *a hard problem*, *hard* é adjetivo; em *work hard*, é advérbio. Já *hardly* não significa simplesmente “de modo duro”: significa “quase não”. Formas aparentadas podem ter sentidos que não se deduzem mecanicamente da terminação.

### Acento e grafia de compostos

Alguns pares diferem pelo acento: *a REcord* (substantivo) e *to reCORD* (verbo); *a PREsent* e *to preSENT*. É uma pista útil, mas não universal. Compostos podem ser uma palavra (*notebook*), duas (*post office*) ou hifenizados (*check-in*); dicionários registram convenções que nem sempre são previsíveis por uma regra única.

### Como cai na prova

- Determine primeiro a classe da lacuna; só depois escolha a terminação.
- Verifique se há negação ou contraste no contexto: *unhappy* e *happy* não são intercambiáveis.
- Cuidado com formas próximas que mudam de significado: *hard* e *hardly*, *economic* e *economical*.
- Em itens de acento e hífen, trate os exemplos como padrões e consulte o contexto, não como leis sem exceção.

summary: A formação de palavras em inglês inclui afixação, composição, conversão, redução (clipping), fusão (blending), formação por iniciais e retroformação. Prefixos antecedem a base e alteram sobretudo o sentido; sufixos vêm depois e frequentemente mudam a classe. Derivação cria palavras relacionadas; flexão marca categorias gramaticais, como plural e tempo verbal. Para exercícios com uma base e uma lacuna, identifique primeiro o sentido e a classe pedidos pela frase, depois escolha a forma e confira grafia e uso. Exemplos-chave: unfair (prefixação), kindness (sufixação), toothbrush (composição), to email (conversão), exam (clipping), brunch (blending), NATO (acrônimo) e edit de editor (retroformação).

flashcards.back: Antes da base: *un* + *fair* forma *unfair*.
Depois da base: *kind* + *-ness* forma *kindness*.
Alteram o sentido, muitas vezes sem mudar a classe, como *happy/unhappy*.
Substantivos abstratos, como *kindness* e *darkness*.
Advérbio; indica o modo de uma ação nesse exemplo.
Composição: combina *tooth* e *brush*.
Mudança de classe sem afixo visível, como *email* substantivo e verbo.
Não. Derivação cria palavra relacionada; flexão marca uma forma gramatical.
Deriva o substantivo *worker* de *work*; o *-s* final marca plural.
Encurtamento de uma palavra, como *examination → exam*.
Fusão de partes de duas palavras, como *breakfast + lunch → brunch*.

flashcards.front: Como se distingue acronym de initialism?
flashcards.back: O acronym é pronunciado como palavra (*NATO*); o initialism, letra por letra (*BBC*).
Criação de uma forma mais curta ao remover uma parte percebida como afixo, como *edit* de *editor*.

flashcards.front: O que pode acontecer ao y final antes de *-ness*?
flashcards.back: Após consoante, frequentemente muda para *i*: *happy → happiness*.

flashcards.front: O que pode acontecer ao e final em *create → creation*?
flashcards.back: O *e* final cai antes do sufixo *-ion*.

flashcards.front: Como identificar a classe necessária numa lacuna?
flashcards.back: Observe a posição da lacuna e a estrutura da frase, além do sentido.

flashcards.front: Qual é a classe de *water* em *water the plants*?
flashcards.back: Verbo por conversão; descreve a ação feita às plantas.

flashcards.front: Qual é a diferença entre *hard* e *hardly*?
flashcards.back: *Hard* pode significar difícil ou intensamente; *hardly* significa quase não.

flashcards.front: O hífen determina sozinho se uma expressão é composta?
flashcards.back: Não. Compostos podem ser juntos, separados ou hifenizados.

flashcards.front: Que classe é *logical* em *a logical answer*?
flashcards.back: Adjetivo que modifica o substantivo *answer*.

tips: Em lacunas, determine sentido e classe gramatical antes de escolher um sufixo.
Memorize exemplos em famílias: *decide, decision, decisive, decisively*.
Separe afixação de composição: *unfair* tem prefixo; *raincoat* combina duas bases.
Para identificar clipping e blending, pergunte se foi encurtada uma palavra ou fundidas partes de duas.
Em compostos, observe qual elemento nomeia a categoria geral: *raincoat* é um tipo de *coat*.
Confira no contexto pares enganadores como *hard/hardly* e *economic/economical*.
traps: Nem toda palavra que começa por *un* contém o prefixo negativo: a sequência sonora e a origem precisam fazer sentido.
Plural em *books* e passado em *walked* são flexão, não necessariamente criação de novo vocábulo.
*Exam* é clipping de uma palavra; não é blending de duas palavras.
*BBC* é pronunciado letra a letra; maiúsculas sozinhas não fazem uma sigla ser acronym.
Uma palavra com hífen não é automaticamente composta por afixos; observe as bases e o sentido.
*Hardly* não é o advérbio regular com o sentido de *hard*: significa quase não.

activeRecall.question: Explique a diferença entre prefixo e sufixo com exemplos.
activeRecall.answer: Prefixo vem antes da base, como *un-* em *unfair*; sufixo vem depois, como *-ness* em *kindness*.

activeRecall.question: Como distinguir derivação de flexão?
activeRecall.answer: Derivação forma palavra relacionada, frequentemente mudando classe (*kind/kindness*); flexão marca gramática (*book/books*, *walk/walked*).

activeRecall.question: Compare composição e conversão.
activeRecall.answer: Composição combina bases reconhecíveis (*toothbrush*); conversão muda a classe da forma sem afixo manifesto (*to email*).

activeRecall.question: Compare clipping e blending.
activeRecall.answer: Clipping encurta uma palavra (*exam*); blending funde partes de duas (*brunch* de *breakfast* e *lunch*).

activeRecall.question: Qual é a diferença entre acronym e initialism?
activeRecall.answer: Acronym é pronunciado como uma palavra, como *NATO*; initialism é pronunciado nomeando as letras, como *BBC*.

activeRecall.question: O que acontece em *editor → edit*?
activeRecall.answer: Retroformação: uma forma mais curta é criada removendo um elemento interpretado como sufixo da forma mais longa.

activeRecall.question: Como resolver uma lacuna de formação de palavras?
activeRecall.answer: Ler o sentido, identificar a classe exigida pela posição sintática, selecionar a forma da família e verificar grafia e uso.

activeRecall.question: Por que *hardly* não deve ser entendido simplesmente como *hard + -ly*?
activeRecall.answer: Porque adquiriu sentido lexical próprio, “quase não”; a terminação não garante que o sentido seja dedutível mecanicamente.

errorConcepts.title: Afixos e sua posição
errorConcepts.summary: Prefixos antecedem a base e sufixos vêm depois; prefixos tendem a alterar sentido e sufixos frequentemente alteram classe, mas o contexto e o vocabulário continuam necessários.

errorConcepts.title: Derivação confundida com flexão
errorConcepts.summary: Derivação forma vocábulo relacionado; flexão marca plural, tempo ou outra categoria gramatical sem necessariamente criar novo lexema.

errorConcepts.title: Processos sem afixação misturados
errorConcepts.summary: Composição combina bases, conversão muda classe sem afixo visível, clipping encurta uma palavra e blending funde segmentos de duas.

errorConcepts.title: Formação por iniciais e retroformação
errorConcepts.summary: Acronym é pronunciado como palavra, initialism letra a letra; back-formation cria forma curta pela remoção de elemento percebido como afixo.

errorConcepts.title: Classe e sentido inferidos só pela terminação
errorConcepts.summary: A posição sintática, o sentido e as combinações usuais determinam a forma adequada; terminações e mudanças ortográficas têm padrões, mas também exceções.

questions.statement: In *unfair*, what is the function and position of *un-*?

options.text: It is a prefix placed before the base and expressing negation.
It is a suffix placed after the base and marking the past tense.
It is a second root that combines with *fair* as a compound.
It is an inflection that marks the plural form of the adjective.
It is a clipping that shortens the original adjective *unfairly*.

questions.explanation: The prefix *un-* occurs before *fair* and gives the adjective a negative or opposite meaning. It is not a suffix, plural marker, compound root, or clipping.

questions.statement: Which word is formed by adding a suffix that commonly creates an abstract noun?

options.text: *Kindness*, with *-ness* added after *kind*.
*Rewrite*, with *re-* added before *write*.
*Raincoat*, by joining the bases *rain* and *coat*.
*Exam*, by shortening the longer word *examination*.
*Water*, used as a verb without a visible affix.

questions.explanation: The suffix *-ness* commonly derives abstract nouns from adjectives, as in *kind → kindness*. The other examples show prefixation, compounding, clipping, and conversion.

questions.statement: In *They carefully checked the figures*, which word class does *carefully* belong to?

options.text: An adverb, because it describes how they checked.
An adjective, because it describes the figures being checked.
A noun, because *care* can name attention or concern.
A verb, because the sentence reports an action in the past.
A preposition, because it connects the subject to the figures.

questions.explanation: *Carefully* modifies the verb *checked* by explaining the manner of checking, so it is an adverb. The sentence's past-tense verb is *checked*, not *carefully*.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which pair best illustrates compounding?

options.text: *Toothbrush*, formed by combining *tooth* and *brush*.
*Teacher*, formed by adding an agent suffix to *teach*.
*Exam*, shortened from the longer word *examination*.
*Unkind*, formed by putting a negative prefix before *kind*.
*To email*, formed by using the noun *email* as a verb.

questions.explanation: A compound joins two bases, as in *tooth + brush*. The alternatives respectively illustrate prefixation, suffixation, clipping, and conversion.

questions.statement: In *Please email me the document*, how is *email* used?

options.text: As a verb by conversion, with no visible affix.
As an adjective describing the document.
As a compound made from two complete nouns.
As a clipped form of the verb *mail*.
As a noun with the plural inflection omitted.

questions.explanation: *Email* is the action requested and takes the object *me the document*, so it functions as a verb. The same form is also a noun in *I sent an email*; this class shift without an affix is conversion.

questions.statement: In *books*, what does the final *-s* normally mark?

options.text: Plural inflection on the noun, rather than a new derived lexeme.
A derivational suffix that changes the noun into an adjective.
A prefix that reverses the meaning of the base noun.
A compound boundary between two independent roots.
A clipping process that removes the end of the noun.

questions.explanation: The inflectional *-s* marks plural. It does not turn *book* into another word class or join it to another base; the lexical item remains *book*, now referring to more than one.

questions.statement: Which example is a clipping?

options.text: *Brunch*, combining parts of *breakfast* and *lunch*.
*NATO*, made from initial letters and pronounced as a word.
*Exam*, shortened from *examination*.
*Babysit*, formed by removing a perceived ending from *babysitter*.
*Raincoat*, formed by joining the bases *rain* and *coat*.

questions.explanation: Clipping shortens one word; *exam* is a familiar shortened form of *examination*. *Brunch* is a blend, *NATO* an acronym, *babysit* a back-formation, and *raincoat* a compound.

questions.statement: Which description fits *brunch*, formed from *breakfast* and *lunch*?

options.text: A blend that fuses parts of two source words.
A prefix added to the beginning of *lunch*.
A suffix added after the complete word *breakfast*.
A clipping that keeps only one unchanged base word.
A regular plural inflection attached to a single noun.

questions.explanation: *Brunch* combines segments of *breakfast* and *lunch*, making it a blend. It is not formed by attaching an affix to just one base.

questions.statement: Which description correctly distinguishes *NATO* from *BBC* in their usual pronunciations?

options.text: Both are clippings because each form is shorter than its source name.
NATO is an acronym said as a word; BBC is an initialism said letter by letter.
NATO is a compound; BBC is a blend of two complete English nouns.
NATO is a back-formation; BBC is a plural inflection with omitted vowels.
Both are initialisms because all forms made from initials are spelled aloud.

questions.explanation: The usual pronunciation matters: *NATO* is spoken as one word, while *BBC* is spoken by naming each letter. Thus they are commonly classified as acronym and initialism, respectively.

questions.statement: In *Her explanation was logical*, which form correctly fills the adjective position?

options.text: *Logic*, the noun naming a system of reasoning.
*Logically*, the adverb describing a manner of reasoning.
*Illogic*, a noun with a negative prefix-like beginning.
*Logical*, the adjective that modifies or describes something.
*Logician*, the noun naming a person who studies logic.

questions.explanation: After the linking verb *was*, the sentence needs a subject complement describing *explanation*. *Logical* is the adjective; the other options are nouns or an adverb.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which statement about the spelling of compounds is accurate?

options.text: Every compound must be written as one uninterrupted word in standard English.
A compound always contains a hyphen between its two lexical bases.
A space proves that the words are a phrase and never a compound.
The spelling form alone always identifies a compound's grammatical class.
Compounds may be closed, open, or hyphenated, depending on convention.

questions.explanation: English compounds appear as one word (*notebook*), separate words (*post office*), or hyphenated forms (*check-in*). A dictionary can confirm conventional spelling when it is uncertain.

questions.statement: In *workers*, how are the ending elements best analyzed?

options.text: Both endings are plural markers attached directly to the verb *work*.
*-er* derives *worker*; the final *-s* marks its plural.
*-er* marks past tense; the final *-s* changes it into an adjective.
The entire ending is a clipping of the compound *work users*.
*-er* is a prefix, and the final *-s* joins a second root.

questions.explanation: First, derivational *-er* forms the person noun *worker* from *work*. Then inflectional *-s* marks more than one worker.

questions.statement: Which word is a typical compound noun in which the second element names the general category?

options.text: *Unfair*, where a negative prefix precedes an adjective base.
*Careless*, where a suffix changes the meaning of a noun base.
*Raincoat*, a kind of coat specified by the first element.
*Exam*, a reduced form of a longer single word.
*To water*, a noun used as a verb without a visible ending.

questions.explanation: In *raincoat*, *coat* identifies the broad category and *rain* specifies its purpose. The other examples represent affixation, clipping, or conversion.

questions.statement: Which process is illustrated by *editor → edit* in a common analysis of the pair?

options.text: Prefixation, because an element is added to the start of the noun.
Compounding, because two complete nouns are joined into a verb.
Clipping, because the source noun is shortened informally in speech.
Back-formation, because a shorter verb is formed by removing an apparent suffix.
Inflection, because the verb receives a marker for the present tense.

questions.explanation: Back-formation creates a shorter lexical form by removing material interpreted as an affix: *edit* is analyzed as formed from *editor*. This is not ordinary inflection or simple informal shortening.

questions.statement: In *They water the plants every morning*, what is *water*?

options.text: An adjective describing the condition of the plants.
A noun functioning as the subject of the clause.
A suffix attached to *plants* to make a compound.
A plural inflection following the subject pronoun.
A verb converted from the noun, taking *the plants* as object.

questions.explanation: *Water* expresses the action and takes *the plants* as its object. The noun form has been used as a verb without adding a visible affix, which is conversion.

questions.statement: Choose the form that correctly completes: *She answered the difficult question ___.*

options.text: *logical*, the adjective used before a noun to describe its kind.
*logic*, the noun naming a system of reasoning.
*illogical*, the negative adjective meaning not reasonable.
*logician*, the noun naming a person who studies reasoning.
*logically*, the adverb modifying how she answered.

questions.explanation: The blank modifies the verb *answered*, so an adverb is needed. *Logically* fits that role; *logical* would describe a noun, and the remaining forms are nouns or an adjective.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which spelling change is illustrated by *happy → happiness*?

options.text: The final *y* after a consonant changes to *i* before *-ness*.
The initial consonant doubles when any suffix is attached.
The suffix moves to the front and becomes a negative prefix.
The final *y* is removed and replaced by the plural ending *-s*.
The two syllables merge through clipping into a shorter word.

questions.explanation: When *-ness* is added to *happy*, the final *y* preceded by a consonant changes to *i*: *happiness*. This is an orthographic adjustment during suffixation.

questions.statement: In *The test was hard, and the students worked hard*, how does the second *hard* function?

options.text: As a noun naming the students' difficult assignment.
As an adverb modifying the verb *worked*, with no *-ly* ending.
As an adjective modifying the plural noun *students*.
As a past-tense verb formed by conversion from *hardness*.
As a preposition linking the workers to the test they took.

questions.explanation: The first *hard* describes the test and is an adjective. The second modifies *worked* and means that the students worked intensely; it functions adverbially despite lacking *-ly*.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which statement best describes the formation of *unhappiness*?

options.text: It is a compound of three independent nouns joined without spaces.
It is an inflected plural form of the adjective *happy*.
It is a clipped form of *unhappy* used in informal conversation.
It is formed only by conversion, with no affix changing the base.
It combines negative prefixation and noun-forming suffixation.

questions.explanation: The base *happy* first takes negative *un-* to form *unhappy*; *-ness* then forms the noun *unhappiness*, with the spelling change *y → i*. Both affixation processes are visible.

questions.statement: What is the main morphological difference between *blackboard* and *blackish*?

options.text: Both are inflected forms because each has more than one syllable.
Both are compounds made by joining two complete free words.
*Blackboard* combines two bases; *blackish* adds the suffix *-ish*.
*Blackboard* is a blend; *blackish* is an acronym pronounced as a word.
*Blackboard* is converted to a verb; *blackish* is its plural form.

questions.explanation: *Blackboard* joins the bases *black* and *board*. *Blackish* contains the suffix *-ish*, which forms an adjective meaning somewhat black or tending toward black.

questions.statement: Which description of *brunch* and *raincoat* is accurate?

options.text: Both are blends because each contains fewer letters than its source expression.
Both are clippings because their first elements are shorter than usual.
Both are inflections because each describes a meal or clothing item.
*Brunch* is a blend of partial forms; *raincoat* joins two complete bases.
*Brunch* is a compound; *raincoat* is a back-formed verb.

questions.explanation: *Brunch* fuses parts of *breakfast* and *lunch*. *Raincoat* preserves the two bases *rain* and *coat* in a compound, even though its spelling is closed.

questions.statement: Which word is most clearly a back-formation in the examples below?

options.text: *Teacher*, created by adding the agent suffix *-er* to *teach*.
*Edit*, analyzed as a verb created from the longer noun *editor*.
*Unfair*, created by attaching a negative prefix to *fair*.
*Exam*, used as a shorter everyday form of *examination*.
*Notebook*, created by combining the nouns *note* and *book*.

questions.explanation: In the common analysis of *editor → edit*, a verb is formed by removing the apparent agent ending from a longer noun. *Teacher* is suffixation, *unfair* prefixation, *exam* clipping, and *notebook* compounding.

questions.statement: In the pair *a REcord / to reCORD*, what does the stress contrast help distinguish?

options.text: The plural and singular forms of the same count noun.
A compound from a phrase written with no hyphen.
A clipping from a blend made from two source words.
The prefix from the root in a regular case of negative affixation.
A noun from a verb, with stress patterns that differ in this pair.

questions.explanation: In this pair, initial stress is typical of the noun *record*, while the verb *record* has final stress. Stress can help identify class in some pairs, but it is a clue rather than a universal rule.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Choose the best completion: *The plan's ___ was discussed at length.* (EFFECT)

options.text: *effective*, the adjective describing a successful plan.
*effectively*, the adverb describing how someone discussed it.
*effect*, the base noun naming a result or influence.
*effectiveness*, the noun naming the quality of being effective.
*effected*, the past-tense verb meaning caused or brought about.

questions.explanation: The possessive *plan's* is followed by a noun as the subject of *was discussed*. *Effectiveness* supplies that noun and names the quality of being effective; the alternatives have other classes or meanings.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *The result was unexpected*, what does the prefix *un-* contribute to *unexpected*?

options.text: It gives *expected* a negative or opposite meaning while retaining adjective class.
It converts the adjective into a plural noun naming several expectations.
It marks the past tense of the verb *expect* without any other ending.
It combines *un* and *expected* as two independent lexical roots.
It removes the suffix from *expectation* to create a shorter verb.

questions.explanation: The prefix *un-* negates or reverses the sense of the adjective *expected*, yielding *unexpected*. The resulting word remains an adjective modifying *result*.

questions.statement: What is the most accurate contrast between *economic* and *economical*?

options.text: They are identical in meaning and can always replace each other.
*Economic* usually relates to the economy; *economical* often means not wasteful.
*Economic* is always a noun; *economical* is always a finite verb.
*Economic* is a plural form; *economical* is its singular spelling.
The first is a clipping, while the second combines two complete roots.

questions.explanation: Both forms are adjectives, but their conventional meanings differ: *economic* commonly concerns the economy, whereas *economical* commonly describes avoiding waste or expense. Context and collocation matter.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: A word-formation item gives *SUCCESS* and the sentence *She completed the project ___.* Which form fits the blank?

options.text: *successful*, an adjective that could describe the completed project.
*success*, a noun that can name a favorable outcome.
*succeed*, a verb that would need a suitable verb position.
*successive*, an adjective meaning following one after another.
*successfully*, an adverb modifying the verb *completed*.

questions.explanation: The blank modifies the action *completed*, so it requires an adverb. *Successfully* is the adverbial form in this word family; the other options are nouns, verbs, or adjectives.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which pair most clearly shows a derivational suffix changing a base into a different word class?

options.text: *book → books*, with plural number marked on the noun.
*walk → walked*, with past tense marked on the verb.
*kind → kindness*, changing an adjective into a noun.
*email → emailed*, with tense marked on a converted verb.
*cat → cats*, with a regular plural ending added to a noun.

questions.explanation: The derivational suffix *-ness* turns adjective *kind* into noun *kindness*. The other examples show inflection for plural or tense, including the inflected converted verb *emailed*.

questions.statement: In a word-formation task, a blank follows *a* and comes before *decision*: *It was a ___ decision.* What type of form is needed?

options.text: A finite verb that agrees with the subject *it* in the past.
An adverb that modifies the adjective *decision* from after it.
A plural noun that names several decisions at the same time.
An adjective that can modify the following noun *decision*.
A preposition that introduces a location or direction phrase.

questions.explanation: The blank is directly before a noun and describes it, so an adjective is needed (for example, *wise* or *difficult*). Word formation questions require this syntactic check before selecting a family member.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: What is the usual difference between *a blackbird* and *a black bird* in stress and interpretation?

options.text: The joined compound often has first-element stress; the open phrase describes any bird that is black.
The joined form is always plural; the spaced form is always singular.
The joined form is a verb; the spaced form is a noun followed by a verb.
The joined form is a clipping; the spaced form is a blend of two colors.
The joined form must have stress on its second part in every English accent.

questions.explanation: The compound *blackbird* commonly names a particular kind of bird and often bears stress on its first element. The phrase *black bird* can describe any bird whose color is black. Stress is a useful clue, not a universal rule.

questions.statement: Which statement about the suffix *-ly* is safest when analyzing English word formation?

options.text: It always converts every adjective into an adverb with a predictable meaning.
It may form adverbs, but the word's role and meaning still need context.
It marks plural nouns whenever the base ends in a consonant.
It is a prefix placed before a word to reverse its meaning.
It combines two free bases into a compound adjective in all cases.

questions.explanation: *-ly* commonly forms adverbs such as *slowly*, but there are exceptions and lexicalized meanings: *friendly* is typically an adjective, and *hardly* means “almost not.” Form and context both matter.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *The old building needs repainting*, which analysis of *repainting* is accurate?

options.text: It is a compound of *repaint* and *painting* with two complete roots.
It is a plural noun because its final letter is *s* in the base form.
It is a clipping of *repaint* used as an informal adjective.
It is a blend of *again* and *painting* with both meanings retained.
It has *re-* for repetition and *-ing* in a verb-derived form.

questions.explanation: The verb *repaint* consists of *re-* plus *paint*, and *repainting* adds the *-ing* form used after *needs* in this construction. The word is not a compound or blend.

questions.statement: In *We had lunch at the campus cafeteria*, what is the most plausible morphological analysis of *lunch*?

options.text: It is a compound formed by joining the words *lunch* and *time*.
It is a suffix that turns the noun *campus* into an adjective.
It is a noun naming a meal, not a blend merely because it is short.
It is a clipping of *breakfast* used to mean the midday meal.
It is an acronym formed from the initial letters of a phrase.

questions.explanation: *Lunch* is an ordinary lexical noun here. A word's short length does not make it clipping; clipping requires a shorter form related to a longer source word, and blending requires parts of two sources.

questions.statement: Which statement correctly compares *teacher* and *edit* in their common formation analyses?

options.text: Both are formed only by adding a suffix to a complete base verb.
Both are compounds because each can be divided into two syllables.
Both are clippings because their final syllables are unstressed.
*Teacher* uses suffixation; *edit* is commonly analyzed as a back-formation from *editor*.
*Teacher* is inflected plural; *edit* is a converted form of *edition*.

questions.explanation: *Teach + -er* derives the agent noun *teacher*. In the common historical/morphological account, *edit* is a back-formation from *editor*, created by removing apparent agent material.

questions.statement: Which form correctly completes: *The instructions were ___, so everyone understood them.* (CLEAR)

options.text: *clearly*, an adverb that would modify an action or adjective.
*clarity*, a noun naming the quality of being clear.
*unclear*, a negative adjective with the opposite meaning.
*clearance*, a noun used for permission or removal of obstacles.
*clear*, an adjective functioning after the linking verb *were*.

questions.explanation: After linking verb *were*, the blank describes the subject *instructions*, so an adjective is required. The context confirms the positive adjective *clear*; *unclear* reverses the needed meaning.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: A candidate sees *beauty* and must form an adjective meaning “having beauty” with *-ful*. Which spelling is standard?

options.text: *beautyful*, keeping the final *y* unchanged before the suffix.
*beautiful*, changing the final *y* to *i* before *-ful*.
*beautifull*, doubling the final *l* after the suffix is added.
*unbeauty*, moving the suffix to the beginning as a prefix.
*beautify*, which is the adjective meaning having beauty.

questions.explanation: The standard spelling is *beautiful*. In this suffixation pattern, final *y* changes to *i*. *Beautify* is a verb meaning to make beautiful, not the adjective requested.

questions.statement: Which analysis of *smog*, from *smoke* and *fog*, is correct?

options.text: It is a regular compound that preserves both complete source words unchanged.
It is a clipping that shortens one source word and discards the other.
It is a blend that fuses parts of both source words into one form.
It is an initialism pronounced by naming the letters S, M, O, and G.
It is a back-formation created by removing a suffix from *smoky*.

questions.explanation: *Smog* fuses segments of *smoke* and *fog*, so it is a blend. A compound such as *raincoat* generally retains the bases more fully.

questions.statement: Which choice is a reliable method for solving a word-formation gap in context?

options.text: Choose the longest family member, because formal tests favor longer words.
Select any word ending in *-ly*, because it must be an adverb in context.
Ignore the sentence meaning and use the first dictionary form listed.
Identify the intended meaning and grammatical slot, then check form and spelling.
Convert every supplied base into a noun, regardless of the surrounding words.

questions.explanation: A sound method checks meaning, grammatical role, and spelling together. Word-family endings are useful clues, but exceptions and context can change the correct form.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *They hardly noticed the change*, what does *hardly* mean in ordinary use?

options.text: They noticed it with great effort and concentration.
They noticed it in a rough or physically harsh manner.
They made the change difficult for other people to notice.
They noticed it repeatedly because the change was important.
They almost did not notice it; *hardly* has a lexicalized meaning.

questions.explanation: In this sentence, *hardly* means “almost not.” It is not simply the regular manner adverb corresponding to the adjective *hard*, which can mean difficult or intense.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: A compound noun *washing machine* contains which pattern?

options.text: A prefix and a suffix attached to the noun *machine*.
A verb-derived *-ing* form followed by the category noun *machine*.
Two plural nouns joined by an apostrophe and a hyphen.
A blend made from *water* and *machine* by overlapping sounds.
A clipping of *washing equipment machine* into two syllables.

questions.explanation: The compound has *washing*, a verb-derived *-ing* form, followed by the head noun *machine*. The complete expression names a type of machine; it is not a blend or a prefix construction.

questions.statement: Which statement about *-er* in English is most accurate?

options.text: It always marks a comparative adjective, as in *taller* and *faster*.
It always marks a person who performs an action, with no other uses.
It can form agent nouns such as *teacher*, but its role depends on the word.
It is a prefix that reverses the meaning of any base it precedes.
It is an acronym marker placed between the initials of a phrase.

questions.explanation: *-er* is used derivationally for agent nouns such as *teach → teacher*, and also inflectionally for comparatives such as *tall → taller*. The word and context determine its function.

questions.statement: Which example shows conversion rather than affixation?

options.text: *Modern → modernize*, with a verb-forming suffix added.
*Fair → unfair*, with a negative prefix added.
*Teach → teacher*, with an agent suffix added.
*Bottle* used as a verb in *bottle the juice*.
*Quick → quickly*, with an adverb-forming suffix added.

questions.explanation: In *bottle the juice*, the noun *bottle* is used as a verb without a visible affix. The other examples add *-ize*, *un-*, *-er*, or *-ly*.

questions.statement: Which form fills the blank with a noun: *Their ___ surprised the whole team.* (ARRIVE)

options.text: *arrive*, the base verb naming the action of reaching a place.
*arrival*, the noun naming the act or event of arriving.
*arriving*, a participial form that can occur in other constructions.
*arrived*, the past form used to report an earlier action.
*arrivable*, an adjective describing a destination that can be reached.

questions.explanation: The possessive *their* can determine a noun phrase, and the blank is its head before *surprised*. *Arrival* is the noun derived from the verb *arrive*.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which description of *NATO* is accurate in its usual pronunciation?

options.text: It is a clipping because the spelling omits most letters of each source word.
It is a blend because two complete words overlap at the same vowel.
It is an initialism because speakers normally name each letter separately.
It is a compound formed by joining the words *national* and *treaty*.
It is an acronym, formed from initials and pronounced as a word.

questions.explanation: *NATO* is formed from initial letters and conventionally pronounced as one word, so it is an acronym. Initialisms such as *BBC* are pronounced letter by letter.

questions.statement: In *The child was careless with the glass*, how is *careless* formed?

options.text: By adding the suffix *-less* to *care* to form an adjective.
By adding the prefix *less-* before *care* to form a noun.
By joining the nouns *car* and *less* into a compound.
By clipping the longer adjective *carefulness* to its first syllable.
By changing the plural noun *cares* into a past-tense verb.

questions.explanation: The suffix *-less* follows *care* and forms the adjective *careless*, meaning without sufficient care. It is not a prefix or a compound of *car* and *less*.

questions.statement: Which description best distinguishes *a record* from *to record*?

options.text: The noun is a plural form, while the verb is its singular counterpart.
The noun is a compound; the verb is a clipping of that compound.
The spelling is the same, but class and stress differ in this pair.
The noun is an acronym; the verb is an initialism said letter by letter.
The noun has a negative prefix; the verb has a plural suffix.

questions.explanation: The spelling remains *record*, while the noun typically has first-syllable stress and the verb final-syllable stress. This is a pronunciation clue associated with a class distinction.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which form completes the sentence with a noun: *The committee discussed the ___ of the proposal.* (IMPORTANT)

options.text: *important*, an adjective that can describe the proposal.
*importantly*, an adverb that modifies a verb or clause.
*unimportant*, a negative adjective meaning not significant.
*importance*, a noun naming the quality of being important.
*import*, a verb meaning to bring goods into a country.

questions.explanation: The article *the* and following *of*-phrase frame a noun phrase. *Importance* is the noun derived from *important* and names a quality or significance.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which statement about the suffix *-ful* is correct in *careful*?

options.text: It is a prefix that comes before *care* and reverses its meaning.
It is an inflection that marks the plural of the noun *care*.
It is a compound root meaning “full” in a separate adjective phrase.
It is a clipping used to shorten the longer word *carefully*.
It follows the base and forms an adjective meaning having care.

questions.explanation: *-ful* is a suffix in *careful* and forms an adjective with the sense of showing or having care. The adverb *carefully* adds another suffix, *-ly*.

questions.statement: In *She is a fast runner*, what is the function of *fast*?

options.text: A noun naming the action performed by the runner.
An adjective modifying the noun *runner*.
A verb converted from the adjective *runner*.
An adverb modifying *is* and expressing frequency.
A suffix attached to *runner* to mark its plural.

questions.explanation: *Fast* occurs before and modifies the noun *runner*, so it is an adjective. The same form can also function adverbially in *run fast*, showing why context matters.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which pair shows the same written form used in two different classes by conversion?

options.text: *kind / kindness*, adjective and noun with a suffix added.
*happy / unhappy*, adjective and its prefixed negative form.
*water* as a noun in *some water* and as a verb in *water the plants*.
*teach / teacher*, verb and agent noun made with a suffix.
*book / books*, singular and plural forms marked by inflection.

questions.explanation: The form *water* functions as a noun in *some water* and as a verb in *water the plants*, with no visible affix change. The other pairs show affixation or inflection.

questions.statement: What is the safest conclusion when a question asks whether a multiword expression is a compound?

options.text: It must be written without spaces to count as a compound in English.
It must contain exactly two nouns and no verb-derived forms.
It must use a hyphen, because open compounds are ordinary phrases.
Its lexical unity and conventional use matter; spelling alone is not decisive.
Its first element must be an adjective and its second a plural noun.

questions.explanation: English compounds may be closed, open, or hyphenated. Their lexical meaning, structure, and conventional dictionary treatment matter more than spacing by itself.

questions.statement: Which expression is an initialism in its usual spoken form?

options.text: *NATO*, spoken as one word from its initial letters.
*Smog*, blended from parts of *smoke* and *fog*.
*Brunch*, blended from parts of two meal names.
*Exam*, shortened from the single word *examination*.
*BBC*, spoken by naming the letters individually.

questions.explanation: *BBC* is normally pronounced letter by letter, so it is an initialism. *NATO* is spoken as a word; *smog* and *brunch* are blends; *exam* is clipping.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses *clean* as a verb by conversion?

options.text: *They clean the kitchen every evening.*
*The kitchen looks clean after the meal.*
*A clean kitchen makes cooking easier.*
*The cleaner arrived before the guests.*
*The cleanliness of the room impressed us.*

questions.explanation: In choice A, *clean* is the action and takes *the kitchen* as its object. The same form is an adjective in B and C; *cleaner* and *cleanliness* contain derivational suffixes.

questions.statement: In *The researchers carefully measured the samples*, which form modifies the verb *measured*?

options.text: *researchers*, a plural noun naming the people doing the work.
*carefully*, an adverb describing the manner of measuring.
*measured*, a verb that serves as the direct object of *carefully*.
*samples*, a noun functioning as the subject of the clause.
*the*, a definite article that modifies the verb's tense.

questions.explanation: *Carefully* modifies *measured*, expressing how the researchers carried out the action. *Researchers* is the subject, *samples* the object, and *the* is a determiner.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which statement best describes the relationship between a base and a word family?

options.text: Every word family member must belong to the same grammatical class.
Only plural and past-tense forms can belong to a word family.
Related forms may differ in class and meaning through word formation.
Family members must share the same spelling and pronunciation exactly.
A base is always the longest form from which shorter words are clipped.

questions.explanation: A word family can include related forms in different classes, such as *decide* (verb), *decision* (noun), *decisive* (adjective), and *decisively* (adverb). Their relationship does not require identical class or form.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: What is the best distinction between *careful* and *carefully*?

options.text: Both are nouns, but the second marks plural number with *-ly*.
*Careful* is an adverb; *carefully* is the past tense of *care*.
Both are compounds created by joining two independent roots.
*-ful* forms an adjective; adding *-ly* then forms an adverb.
*-ful* is a prefix and *-ly* removes the negative meaning.

questions.explanation: *Care + -ful* forms the adjective *careful*. Adding *-ly* yields the adverb *carefully*, which can modify a verb such as *drive carefully*.

questions.statement: Which form completes: *The machine operates ___ even in cold weather.* (RELIABLE)

options.text: *reliable*, an adjective that can describe the machine itself.
*reliability*, a noun naming dependable performance.
*unreliable*, an adjective meaning not dependable.
*rely*, a verb meaning depend on someone or something.
*reliably*, an adverb modifying how the machine operates.

questions.explanation: The blank modifies the verb *operates*, so an adverb is required. *Reliably* supplies that form and agrees with the positive meaning of the sentence.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which example contains a derivational prefix that expresses repetition?

options.text: *Rewrite*, with *re-* meaning to write again.
*Kindness*, with *-ness* forming an abstract noun.
*Teacher*, with *-er* forming an agent noun.
*Books*, with *-s* marking plural number.
*Brunch*, with parts of two source words fused together.

questions.explanation: The prefix *re-* in *rewrite* means again. The other examples show derivational suffixation, plural inflection, and blending.

questions.statement: In *The singer gave an impressive performance*, what is *impressive*?

options.text: A noun naming the person who performed for the audience.
A verb in the past tense describing the singer's action.
An adjective modifying the noun *performance*.
An adverb modifying the verb *gave* from the end of the clause.
A plural inflection attached to the noun *impression*.

questions.explanation: *Impressive* precedes and describes *performance*, so it is an adjective. Its suffix *-ive* helps form an adjective related to *impress*.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: A candidate must form a verb from *simple* meaning “make simple.” Which word-formation result fits?

options.text: *simpleness*, a noun naming the quality of being simple.
*simply*, an adverb meaning in a simple manner.
*simpler*, a comparative adjective meaning more simple.
*simplify*, a verb formed with *-ify* and meaning make simple.
*unsimple*, a prefixed adjective meaning not simple.

questions.explanation: The instruction asks for a verb meaning “make simple.” The suffix *-ify* forms *simplify*; the alternatives are nouns or adjectives.

questions.statement: Which statement about *un-* and *in-* is most accurate?

options.text: They are inflectional endings that always mark plural nouns.
They are prefixes that can express negation, with forms such as *im-* and *il-*.
They are suffixes that must follow every adjective in English.
They join two free bases and therefore always make compounds.
They are acronyms pronounced as complete English words.

questions.explanation: Negative prefixes include *un-* and *in-*, with related forms such as *im-* in *impossible* and *il-* in *illegal*. The precise choice is lexicalized and should not be applied mechanically to every base.

questions.statement: What does the word-formation process in *motel* most plausibly involve?

options.text: A regular plural ending attached to the noun *mote*.
A prefix added to the complete word *hotel* to reverse its sense.
A clipped form of only one source word, with no second source.
A compound that preserves both complete words with a space.
A blend combining parts of *motor* and *hotel*.

questions.explanation: *Motel* fuses segments of *motor* and *hotel*, so it is a blend. It is not simply a shortened form of only one of those source words.

questions.statement: Which statement about *-en* in *widen* is correct?

options.text: It is a prefix that means the opposite of the adjective *wide*.
It is a plural ending used because *wide* names more than one thing.
It is a verb-forming suffix that derives a verb from the adjective.
It is a clipping process that removes the first syllable of *wideness*.
It combines *wide* and a second independent noun into a compound.

questions.explanation: The suffix *-en* forms the verb *widen* from the adjective *wide*, meaning make or become wider. It follows the base and is not a plural marker.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses *daily* as an adverb rather than an adjective?

options.text: *The daily newspaper arrived before breakfast.*
*She takes a daily walk after work.*
*Their daily routine includes a short meeting.*
*The shop opens daily at nine in the morning.*
*We read the daily report together at lunch.*

questions.explanation: In D, *daily* modifies the verb phrase *opens* and means every day, so it functions as an adverb. In A, B, C, and E it modifies a following noun and functions as an adjective.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: A learner sees *care* and the sentence *The driver reacted ___ to the warning.* Which form fits the slot and meaning?

options.text: *careless*, an adjective meaning without care, used before a noun.
*carefully*, an adverb meaning with care, modifying *reacted*.
*carefulness*, a noun naming the quality of being cautious.
*care*, a noun that names attention and serves as the verb's object.
*uncaring*, an adjective that describes a person lacking concern.

questions.explanation: The blank modifies the verb *reacted*, and the context indicates a careful manner. *Carefully* is the adverb; *careless* and *uncaring* express a different class or meaning.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which statement best describes the role of a base in word formation?

options.text: It is necessarily the longest form in a family and cannot take affixes.
It is a grammatical ending that marks tense on every English verb.
It is always a compound made from two complete words.
It is the form to which a word-building element may be attached.
It is a spoken abbreviation that must be written in capital letters.

questions.explanation: A base is the form that an affix or another word-building process operates on. For instance, *kind* is a base in *unkind* and *kindness*; a base need not be the longest family member.

questions.statement: In *Her answer was completely unexpected*, what is the role of *completely*?

options.text: A noun naming the completeness of the answer.
An adjective modifying the noun *answer* directly.
An adverb modifying the adjective *unexpected*.
A past-tense verb whose object is the word *unexpected*.
A plural marker attached to the noun *expectation*.

questions.explanation: *Completely* is an adverb of degree modifying the adjective *unexpected*. Its position before an adjective and its *-ly* form are consistent with this function.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *They redesigned the old website*, what does the prefix *re-* contribute to *redesigned*?

options.text: It marks a plural noun because the website has several pages.
It means that the design action was done again or anew.
It converts the adjective *designed* into a noun naming a person.
It is a suffix following the base and marking the simple past.
It joins *red* and *esigned* as two independent lexical bases.

questions.explanation: The prefix *re-* commonly expresses repetition or doing something again. In *redesigned*, it precedes *design* while the past-tense ending *-ed* follows the verb base.

questions.statement: Which pair illustrates a spelling change in which a final *e* is dropped before a suffix?

options.text: *create → creation*, where the final *e* disappears before *-ion*.
*happy → happiness*, where *y* changes to *i* before *-ness*.
*care → careful*, where the base retains its final *e*.
*book → books*, where plural *-s* follows the noun unchanged.
*wide → widen*, where a verb-forming suffix follows the base.

questions.explanation: In *create → creation*, the final *e* is dropped before *-ion*. The other examples illustrate a *y → i* change, retention of *e*, regular plural marking, or verb suffixation.

questions.statement: In *Her response was friendly*, which statement is correct about the form and class of *friendly*?

options.text: It is an adverb because every word ending in *-ly* modifies a verb.
It is a plural noun because *-ly* is a variant of the plural ending.
It is a verb formed by conversion from the noun *friendliness*.
It is an adjective describing *response*; the ending alone does not decide class.
It is a compound made by joining the free words *friend* and *ly*.

questions.explanation: *Friendly* modifies the noun *response*, so it is an adjective. Although *-ly* often forms adverbs, it also occurs in adjectives, which shows why sentence function matters.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which option best explains why *blackboard* can be treated as a compound even though it is written as one word?

options.text: A closed spelling prevents a word from containing more than one morpheme.
A compound requires a hyphen, so *blackboard* cannot be one.
It combines the recognizable bases *black* and *board* into a lexical unit.
It is a clipping because the space between the bases was removed.
It is an acronym because the first letters form the sequence B and B.

questions.explanation: Compounds can be written closed. *Blackboard* contains the recognizable bases *black* and *board* forming a lexical unit; spacing and hyphens do not determine compound status by themselves.

questions.statement: Which distinction between *ad* and *brunch* is correct?

options.text: Both are acronyms because their written forms contain fewer letters.
*Ad* is clipping from one word; *brunch* blends parts of two words.
*Ad* is a blend; *brunch* is the regular plural of *brunch*.
Both are compounds preserving two complete source words.
*Ad* is a back-formation; *brunch* is a past-tense verb.

questions.explanation: *Ad* is a shortened form of the single word *advertisement*. *Brunch* fuses parts of *breakfast* and *lunch*, so it is a blend.

questions.statement: Choose the correct completion: *The instructions were ___ written and easy to follow.* (CLEAR)

options.text: *clear*, an adjective that could describe the instructions before a noun.
*clarity*, a noun naming the quality of being clear.
*unclear*, an adjective that contradicts the positive context.
*clearance*, a noun meaning authorization or removal.
*clearly*, an adverb modifying the manner of writing.

questions.explanation: The blank modifies *written*, so an adverb is required. *Clearly* expresses how the instructions were written and matches the positive context.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: Which statement about derivational suffixes is accurate?

options.text: They always mark only tense or number and never affect lexical meaning.
They occur before the base and are therefore another name for prefixes.
They can create related words and often change a word's grammatical class.
They combine two independent bases without changing their spelling.
They are limited to clipping, acronyms, and other shortened forms.

questions.explanation: Derivational suffixes follow a base and form related lexical items, often changing class, as in *kind → kindness* or *quick → quickly*. Tense and number are typical inflectional functions.

questions.statement: What is the most accurate analysis of *babysit*, commonly related to *babysitter*?

options.text: A plural inflection is removed from a noun to make the same noun singular.
A prefix is added to the adjective *baby* to express negation.
A blend fuses *baby* with the verb *sit* by overlapping their sounds.
A verb is formed by removing the apparent agent ending from a longer form.
A clipping shortens *babysitting* but leaves its grammatical class unchanged.

questions.explanation: *Babysit* is commonly treated as a back-formation from *babysitter*: the verb is formed by removing the apparent agent suffix *-er* from the longer noun.

questions.statement: Which sentence contains *daily* as an adjective?

options.text: *The team meets daily before the office opens.*
*The newspaper is delivered daily to subscribers.*
*They exercise daily when the weather is good.*
*The clinic operates daily except on public holidays.*
*She reads the daily newspaper on her commute.*

questions.explanation: In E, *daily* modifies the noun *newspaper* and functions as an adjective. In A–D it modifies the action or clause and means every day adverbially.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In a standard word-formation exercise, what should a candidate do after choosing a form with the right grammatical class?

options.text: Check whether its meaning fits the sentence and its spelling is conventional.
Ignore the sentence meaning because class alone determines the answer.
Replace it with the longest available word in the family.
Add a plural ending even when the blank is an adverb or adjective.
Assume every suffix has exactly one meaning and no lexical exceptions.

questions.explanation: Class is only one check. The candidate must also confirm that the meaning fits and that the word has the conventional spelling and usage required by the sentence.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *unfair*, the prefix *un-* comes before the base and commonly gives it a negative or opposite meaning.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. *Un-* is a prefix because it precedes *fair*; *unfair* means not fair or the opposite of fair. The adjective remains an adjective after this prefix is added.

questions.statement: In *kindness*, the element *-ness* is a prefix attached before the base *kind*.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *-ness* is a suffix and appears after *kind*. It commonly derives an abstract noun from an adjective, as in *kind → kindness*.

questions.statement: In *books*, the final *-s* normally marks grammatical plural rather than creating a new word class.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. The plural ending changes the number of the noun *book*; it does not turn the noun into an adjective or verb. This is inflection rather than derivation.

questions.statement: The word *toothbrush* is formed by adding the suffix *-brush* to the base *tooth*.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *Toothbrush* is a compound of two lexical bases, *tooth* and *brush*. A suffix is a bound element such as *-ness*, not an independent word like *brush*.

questions.statement: In *Please email me the file*, *email* is used as a verb without a visible derivational affix.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. *Email* names the action and takes an object, *me the file*. Using a noun form as a verb without a visible affix is conversion, also called zero derivation.

questions.statement: *Exam* is a blend because it combines parts of *examination* and another source word.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *Exam* is a clipping, a shortened form of the single word *examination*. A blend such as *brunch* fuses segments from two source words.

questions.statement: *Brunch* combines parts of *breakfast* and *lunch*, so it is a blend.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. A blend fuses segments of two source words; *brunch* takes material from *breakfast* and *lunch*. It differs from a compound such as *raincoat*, which preserves both bases more fully.

questions.statement: An acronym such as *NATO* is usually spoken as one word, while an initialism such as *BBC* is spoken letter by letter.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. The pronunciation distinguishes the common labels: *NATO* is said as a word, whereas *BBC* is pronounced by naming the individual letters.

questions.statement: Back-formation forms *editor* by adding the suffix *-or* to the already existing verb *edit*.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado in the commonly cited direction of this pair: *edit* is analyzed as a verb formed by removing the apparent agent ending from *editor*. Adding *-or* to a verb would be suffixation instead.

questions.statement: The ending *-ly* always guarantees that a word is an adverb, so *friendly* must be an adverb in *a friendly reply*.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *Friendly* modifies the noun *reply*, so it is an adjective. Although *-ly* commonly forms adverbs, the ending alone cannot determine a word's class.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *hardly noticed*, *hardly* means that the person noticed something with great effort.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *Hardly* usually means “almost not,” so *hardly noticed* means the person almost did not notice. *Hard* can mean intensely, but *hardly* has a distinct lexicalized meaning.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: A compound such as *post office* must be written as one closed word to count as a compound.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. English compounds can be written closed (*notebook*), open (*post office*), or hyphenated (*check-in*). Spacing alone does not decide whether a lexical expression is a compound.

questions.statement: In *workers*, *-er* can form the agent noun *worker*, and the final *-s* marks plural.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. The derivational suffix *-er* forms a person noun from *work*. The later plural inflection *-s* indicates more than one worker, so both processes occur in sequence.

questions.statement: The noun *blackboard* cannot be a compound because English compounds always include a hyphen.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *Blackboard* is a closed compound made from *black* and *board*. Compounds may be written as one word, separately, or with a hyphen, depending on convention.

questions.statement: The prefix *re-* in *rewrite* can express doing the action again.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. *Re-* is placed before *write* and commonly expresses repetition: *rewrite* means write again. The prefix does not mark tense or plural number.

questions.statement: In *The team worked hard*, *hard* must be an adjective because adjectives always end in *-ly*.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. *Hard* modifies the verb *worked* and functions adverbially here, despite having no *-ly* ending. English class cannot always be identified from a suffix alone.
questions.section: 4. Escolha da forma e leitura em contexto

questions.statement: In *readable*, the suffix *-able* follows the base *read* and forms an adjective.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. *-able* follows the verb base *read* and derives the adjective *readable*, meaning able to be read. Its position after the base identifies it as a suffix.

questions.statement: Adding *-ness* to *happy* commonly changes the final *y* to *i*, producing *happiness*.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. When final *y* follows a consonant, it often changes to *i* before *-ness*: *happy → happiness*. This is a spelling adjustment accompanying suffixation.
